title: [Bug]: HAL_DMA_Abort may fail with timeout on certain optimization levels
body:
### Bug Summary

HAL_DMA_Abort may fail on DMA_SxCR_EN at the H7 (at least M4 Core) on certain GCC optimization levels

### Detailed Description

Dear ST support,

I found an interesting but hard-to-track bug in the HAL_DMA_Abort function which seems to be bus timing related:

The function `HAL_DMA_Abort` fails (in my code) on the check if the DMA is effectively disabled monitoring the `DMA_SxCR_EN` register. This happens on the DMA2 + M4 core in the H745 dual core but the M7 core might be affected as well. When it fails it returns a `HAL_ERROR` (ErrorCode = HAL_DMA_ERROR_TIMEOUT, State = HAL_DMA_STATE_ERROR).

But this fails only on the following (GCC) optimization levels:
-  -O2, -O3, -Ofast, -Os, -Oz
It does not fail on the following optimization levels:
- -O0, -O1, -Og

Here is a potential fix: It does never fail if there is a single `__NOP();` between [`__HAL_DMA_DISABLE(hdma);`](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx-hal-driver/blob/a1996eed9172b59887bafaaa0ea1816ea14d48b5/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_dma.c#L806) and [`if(IS_DMA_DMAMUX_ALL_INSTANCE(hdma->Instance) != 0U)`](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx-hal-driver/blob/a1996eed9172b59887bafaaa0ea1816ea14d48b5/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_dma.c#L825).

I will not try to dive deeper into this bug. You will be able to diagnose and improve this situation far better at STM.

### Expected Behavior

_No response_

### Actual Behavior

_No response_

### Environment

_No response_

### Severity

Normal

title: [Bug]: `HAL_SD_ConfigWideBusOperation` applies UHS clock bypass on 3.3V bus when `USE_SD_TRANSCEIVER == 0`
body:
### Bug Summary

When `USE_SD_TRANSCEIVER` is **not set** (no 1.8V voltage transceiver), `HAL_SD_ConfigWideBusOperation()` can still apply `ClockDiv = 0` (clock bypass) for cards that report `CARD_ULTRA_HIGH_SPEED` capability. This results in the SDMMC peripheral running at full kernel clock speed (e.g., 100 MHz) on a **3.3V bus**, far exceeding the SD specification limit of 50 MHz for High Speed mode at 3.3V.

### Detailed Description

## Affected Function

[`HAL_SD_ConfigWideBusOperation()` in `Src/stm32h7xx_hal_sd.c`](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx-hal-driver/blob/a1996eed9172b59887bafaaa0ea1816ea14d48b5/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_sd.c#L1723)

## Root Cause

There is an inconsistency between `HAL_SD_ConfigSpeedBusOperation()` and `HAL_SD_ConfigWideBusOperation()`:

### `ConfigSpeedBusOperation` — correctly guarded

[`HAL_SD_ConfigSpeedBusOperation()`](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx-hal-driver/blob/a1996eed9172b59887bafaaa0ea1816ea14d48b5/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_sd.c#L1866) uses [`#if (USE_SD_TRANSCEIVER != 0U)`](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx-hal-driver/blob/a1996eed9172b59887bafaaa0ea1816ea14d48b5/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_sd.c#L1878) to separate UHS and non-UHS code paths. When there is **no transceiver**, the [`SDMMC_SPEED_MODE_AUTO` case](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx-hal-driver/blob/a1996eed9172b59887bafaaa0ea1816ea14d48b5/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_sd.c#L1985) correctly limits the card to **SDR25 (High Speed, 50 MHz)** — it does **not** attempt UHS voltage switching.

### `ConfigWideBusOperation` — NOT guarded (the bug)

[`HAL_SD_ConfigWideBusOperation()`](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx-hal-driver/blob/a1996eed9172b59887bafaaa0ea1816ea14d48b5/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_sd.c#L1723) has **no** `USE_SD_TRANSCEIVER` check. It decides the clock divider based solely on `hsd->SdCard.CardSpeed`:

```c
// Line 1793-1794 — no USE_SD_TRANSCEIVER guard
else if (hsd->SdCard.CardSpeed == CARD_ULTRA_HIGH_SPEED)
{
    /* UltraHigh speed SD card,user Clock div */
    Init.ClockDiv = hsd->Init.ClockDiv;   // user value (typically 0) → bypass!
}
```

[Source: stm32h7xx_hal_sd.c L1793–L1794](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx-hal-driver/blob/a1996eed9172b59887bafaaa0ea1816ea14d48b5/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_sd.c#L1793-L1794)

When `hsd->Init.ClockDiv == 0` (which means "auto-decide"), this blindly passes `0` to the CLKCR register, setting **CLKDIV = 0 (bypass mode)** — the SDMMC clock runs at full kernel clock frequency (e.g., 100 MHz) with no division.

## Bug Sequence

1. **`HAL_SD_Init()`** identifies the card and sets `hsd->SdCard.CardSpeed = CARD_ULTRA_HIGH_SPEED` based on the card's SCR register / CMD6 switch response.

2. **`HAL_SD_ConfigSpeedBusOperation(SDMMC_SPEED_MODE_AUTO)`** correctly detects no transceiver is present and only negotiates **SDR25 (High Speed)**. However, it does **not** update `hsd->SdCard.CardSpeed` — it remains `CARD_ULTRA_HIGH_SPEED`.

3. **`HAL_SD_ConfigWideBusOperation()`** reads `hsd->SdCard.CardSpeed == CARD_ULTRA_HIGH_SPEED` and applies `Init.ClockDiv = hsd->Init.ClockDiv = 0` → **bypass mode (100 MHz on 3.3V bus)**.

## Impact

- The SDMMC bus runs at **100 MHz on 3.3V signaling**, exceeding the SD specification maximum of **50 MHz for High Speed** and **25 MHz for Default Speed** at 3.3V.
- This violates the SD Physical Layer Specification and may cause **data corruption**, **CRC errors**, or **card damage** on some cards.
- It happens to work on some embedded SD NAND chips (e.g., ZBIT, MKFD) that tolerate overclocking on short BGA traces, masking the bug.
- The issue is particularly insidious because the speed negotiation in `ConfigSpeedBusOperation` is correct — only the clock divider in `ConfigWideBusOperation` is wrong.

## Reproduction

1. Use any STM32H7 board **without** a 1.8V voltage transceiver (`USE_SD_TRANSCEIVER == 0`).
2. Insert an SD card that reports UHS-I capability (common in SDHC/SDXC cards and embedded SD NAND).
3. Initialize with `hsd->Init.ClockDiv = 0` (auto-decide).
4. Call `HAL_SD_Init()`, then `HAL_SD_ConfigSpeedBusOperation(SDMMC_SPEED_MODE_AUTO)`, then `HAL_SD_ConfigWideBusOperation()`.
5. Read `SDMMC_CLKCR` register → `CLKDIV = 0` (bypass), confirmed by oscilloscope showing 100 MHz on CLK line.

### Register dump confirming the issue

```
SDMMC1_CLKCR:  0x00025000
  CLKDIV:      0          ← bypass, no division
  WIDBUS:      01 (4-bit)
  BUSSPEED:    0  (DS/HS)

RCC D1CCIPR SDMMCSEL: PLL2_R = 100 MHz
→ SDMMC_CK = 100 MHz (should be 50 MHz max for HS at 3.3V)
```

## Suggested Fix

**Option A** — Guard `ConfigWideBusOperation` with `USE_SD_TRANSCEIVER`:

```c
else if (hsd->SdCard.CardSpeed == CARD_ULTRA_HIGH_SPEED)
{
#if (USE_SD_TRANSCEIVER != 0U)
    /* UltraHigh speed SD card, user Clock div */
    Init.ClockDiv = hsd->Init.ClockDiv;
#else
    /* No transceiver: UHS not possible, fall back to High Speed clock */
    if (hsd->Init.ClockDiv == 0U)
    {
        Init.ClockDiv = sdmmc_clk / (2U * SD_HIGH_SPEED_FREQ);
    }
    else
    {
        Init.ClockDiv = hsd->Init.ClockDiv;
    }
#endif
}
```

**Option B** — Update `CardSpeed` in `ConfigSpeedBusOperation` when downgrading:

In the no-transceiver path of `ConfigSpeedBusOperation`, after successfully switching to SDR25:

```c
if (SD_SwitchSpeed(hsd, SDMMC_SDR25_SWITCH_PATTERN) != HAL_SD_ERROR_NONE)
{
    hsd->ErrorCode |= HAL_SD_ERROR_UNSUPPORTED_FEATURE;
    status = HAL_ERROR;
}
else
{
    hsd->SdCard.CardSpeed = CARD_HIGH_SPEED;  // reflect actual negotiated speed
}
```

## Environment

- **MCU**: STM32H747
- **HAL version**: v1.13.0
- **Transceiver**: None (`USE_SD_TRANSCEIVER == 0`)
- **SD cards tested**: ZBIT SDNAND (ZBSD), MKFD SDNAND (MK) — both report `CARD_ULTRA_HIGH_SPEED`
- **SDMMC kernel clock**: PLL2_R = 100 MHz

### Expected Behavior

when USE_SD_TRANSCEIVER=0 , cap the speed to 50Mhz

### Actual Behavior

when USE_SD_TRANSCEIVER=0 , blindly apply 100M bypass from sdmmc_kernel clk

### Environment

_No response_

### Severity

Major

title: AES CCM Encryption and Decryption operations output overflow
body:
**Describe the set-up**
Custom board with STM32H730XX.

AES CCM encryption and decryption are performed with settings:
```
DataType = CRYP_DATATYPE_8B
DataWidthUnit  = CRYP_DATAWIDTHUNIT_BYTE
KeySize = CRYP_KEYSIZE_128B
HeaderWidthUnit = CRYP_HEADERWIDTHUNIT_BYTE
```

**Describe the bug**
There is an overflow in the HAL’s `CRYP_AESCCM_Process` when the payload length is not a multiple of 4 bytes. No masking is applied when the output block is read from the HW output FIFO, that leads to data being written beyond the output buffer.

Depending on where the buffer is and if it accounts for required alignment the overflow might lead to different consequences.

An encryption overflow example below uses the following key, nonce, ad (_they don't matter much for the issue_):
```
key[] = {
	0xf5, 0x95, 0x5f, 0xe1,
	0xdd, 0x84, 0x74, 0xfd,
	0x85, 0xe5, 0xfc, 0xf8,
	0x20, 0x33, 0x70, 0x01
}
nonce[] = {
	0x26, 0xd4, 0xf1, 0xfc,
	0x00, 0x01, 0x00, 0x00,
	0x00, 0x00 ,0x00 ,0x02
}
ad[]= {
	0x00, 0x01, 0x00, 0x00,
	0x00, 0x00 ,0x00 ,0x02,
	0x15, 0xfe, 0xfd, 0x00,
	0x02
}
```

Given 15 bytes payload:
```
plaintext[] = {
	0x01, 0x02, 0x03, 0x04,
	0x05, 0x06, 0x07, 0x08,
	0x09, 0x0A, 0x0B, 0x0C,
	0x0D, 0x0E, 0x0F
}
```
it is expected to produce 15 bytes ciphertext:
```
expected_output[15] = {
	0xf8, 0x75, 0xe9, 0x1c,
	0xe7, 0xb5, 0xf2, 0x7c,
	0x1c, 0x54, 0x6a, 0xd9,
	0x87, 0x92, 0xca
}
```

in reality it produces 16 bytes where the first 15 bytes are correct (_as expected_), but an extra 16th byte - `0x3e` is written:
```
0x24029898   xf8   0x75   0xe9   0x1c   0xe7   0xb5   0xf2   0x7c
0x240298a0   x1c   0x54   0x6a   0xd9   0x87   0x92   0xca   0x3e
0x240298a8   x00   0x00   0x00   0x00
```
If we reduce the plaintext to 13 bytes, then we will get  3 extra bytes.

Some libraries (_e.g. MbedTLS_) use a single shared buffer that contains both the plaintext/ciphertext and the authentication tag. Because of the overflow, the trailing bytes overwrite the tag section, resulting in tag corruption during decryption.

**How To Reproduce**
Perform AES‑CCM encryption and/or decryption with the HAL where the payload length is not a multiple of 4, and direct the result into a larger empty buffer than the payload.
The output will overflow the expected payload area and corrupt subsequent bytes.

**Additional context**
A similar approach to https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx-hal-driver/commit/863ab1fdaa904c8f6630c91acdb455cf99e37473 is required for the CCM parts upon reading data out to avoid an overflow.

The `CRYP_AESCCM_Process` should account for `CRYP_DATATYPE_8B` and avoid filling the output buffer as
`      *(uint32_t *)(hcryp->pCrypOutBuffPtr + hcryp->CrypOutCount) = temp[index];`.

I did a research with Claude on this topic, TL;DR basically the standard did not explictly say set or not set length for short packet, it is up to perpherial default which varies, this is a design flaw in my opinion, and many other manufactures are either clamp to 1byte or just set length anyways to avoid this issue, ST should do the same instead of "it is not specified in the standard"


Research result:

---


# STM32 HAL DSI Read Threshold: A Likely Bug in MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE Handling

**The STM32 HAL's `datasize > 2U` threshold for sending MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE appears incorrect per the MIPI DSI specification.** When reading exactly 2 bytes, the HAL does not send this command, potentially causing the display peripheral to return only 1 byte. The correct condition should likely be `datasize > 1U` or `datasize >= 2U` to ensure 2-byte reads work reliably. Other vendors like Samsung/Exynos and even other STM32 HAL functions always send MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE unconditionally, avoiding this edge case.

## The core issue: peripheral default behavior is undefined

The MIPI DSI specification (versions 1.0 through DSI-2) does **not mandate a universal default** for the maximum return packet size when the `Set Maximum Return Packet Size` command (Data Type **0x37**) is never issued. This critical detail is explicitly left as **peripheral-dependent behavior**. Most display controller ICs default to returning only **1 byte** if not instructed otherwise, as this is the most conservative assumption.

The DSI short read response packet types illustrate why this matters. For **1 byte**, peripherals use Generic Short Read Response (0x11) or DCS Short Read Response (0x21). For **2 bytes**, they use types 0x12 or 0x22 respectively. For 3+ bytes, Long Read Responses (0x1A or 0x1C) are required. The peripheral selects the response type based on *both* the actual data length available *and* the MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE constraint—whichever is smaller dictates the response.

## STM32 HAL implementation uses a problematic threshold

The STM32 HAL DSI driver across all STM32 families (F4, F7, H7, L4, U5) uses identical logic:

```c
if (datasize > 2U)
{
    /* set max return packet size */
    DSI_ShortWrite(hdsi, ChannelNbr, DSI_MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE, 
                   ((datasize) & 0xFFU), (((datasize) >> 8U) & 0xFFU));
}
```

This means when `datasize == 2`, the command **is not sent**. If the peripheral defaults to 1 byte (as many do), it will use a 1-byte short read response (0x21) instead of a 2-byte response (0x22), returning only half the requested data. The STM32 HAL appears to assume peripherals always support 2-byte short reads without explicit configuration—an assumption the specification does not guarantee.

## Vendor implementations reveal divergent approaches

A survey of major vendor implementations shows significant variation in handling this threshold:

| Vendor/Driver | Threshold Logic | MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE Sent For |
|---------------|-----------------|------------------------------|
| **STM32 HAL** | `datasize > 2` | Only reads ≥3 bytes |
| **Qualcomm MSM** | `rlen <= 2` check | Only reads >2 bytes |
| **Samsung Exynos** | Unconditional | Every read operation |
| **Linux DRM core** | Delegated | Panel driver responsibility |
| **MediaTek** | Delegated | Panel driver responsibility |
| **Synopsys DW-DSI** | Delegated | Panel driver responsibility |

Samsung's Exynos driver takes the **most conservative approach**, always sending MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE regardless of read size. Qualcomm's MSM driver uses similar logic to STM32 but assumes short reads (≤2 bytes) work without explicit configuration. The Linux kernel core delegates this entirely to panel drivers, which must call `mipi_dsi_set_maximum_return_packet_size()` explicitly before reads.

## The specification's response type selection mechanism

According to MIPI DSI v1.1 Section 8.2, the peripheral follows this decision tree when responding to read commands:

1. Determine how much data the register actually contains
2. Clamp this value to MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE (if set)
3. If resulting size ≤ 2 bytes: use Short Read Response (1-byte or 2-byte variant)
4. If resulting size > 2 bytes: use Long Read Response with actual payload

When MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE is **not configured**, the peripheral uses its internal default—which the specification allows to be **as low as 1 byte**. This explains why 2-byte reads can fail: the peripheral has no indication that 2 bytes are expected and may cap its response at its default of 1 byte.

## Documented STM32 HAL DSI issues support this analysis

The ST Community forums contain multiple reports of DSI read problems that align with this analysis:

- **HAL_LOCK bug** (fixed): Early HAL versions had a nested lock issue where `DSI_ShortWrite()` called from within `HAL_DSI_Read()` would deadlock. ST's release notes confirm: *"Fix read multibyte issue: remove extra call to HAL_UNLOCK from DSI_ShortWrite() API."*

- **BTA not enabled**: Developers discovered that `HAL_DSI_ConfigFlowControl(hdsi, DSI_FLOW_CONTROL_BTA)` must be called before DSI reads work at all—a prerequisite not clearly documented.

- **Reads returning only 1 byte**: Multiple forum posts describe scenarios where multi-byte reads return incomplete data, with users reporting *"data are read not completely, only 1 byte from four."*

## Recommended fixes and workarounds

**Option 1: Change the threshold condition** (requires HAL modification)
```c
// Current code (potentially buggy)
if (datasize > 2U)

// Recommended fix - always send for 2+ bytes  
if (datasize > 1U)

// Alternative fix - always send unconditionally
// (matches Samsung/Exynos approach, slight overhead for 1-byte reads)
```

**Option 2: Pre-configure MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE manually**
Before calling `HAL_DSI_Read()` for 2-byte reads, manually send:
```c
HAL_DSI_ShortWrite(&hdsi, 0, DSI_MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE, 0x02, 0x00);
```

**Option 3: Always send MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE before every read**
Wrap `HAL_DSI_Read()` with a function that unconditionally sends the command first, matching the Samsung/Exynos approach.

## Technical rationale for the recommended fix

The threshold `datasize > 2U` is logically flawed because short read responses cover **both** 1-byte and 2-byte cases. The STM32 code **_implicitly assumes_** peripherals will automatically use 2-byte responses when 2 bytes are available, but this requires the peripheral to know 2 bytes are expected. Without MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE, a peripheral defaulting to 1 byte has no way to know a 2-byte response is acceptable.

The correct logic should be: send MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE whenever the requested size exceeds the **minimum guaranteed default** of 1 byte. This means `datasize > 1U` or simply always sending the command. The slight protocol overhead (one additional 4-byte short packet) is negligible compared to the reliability gained.

## Conclusion

The STM32 HAL DSI driver's `datasize > 2U` threshold represents a **latent bug** that manifests when reading exactly 2 bytes from peripherals that default to 1-byte maximum return packet sizes. While some displays may work due to having larger defaults, the implementation is not specification-compliant for the general case. Developers encountering 2-byte DSI read failures should modify the threshold to `datasize > 1U` or manually send MAX_RETURN_PKT_SIZE before reads. Samsung's approach of unconditionally sending the command remains the most robust solution, adding minimal overhead while ensuring cross-peripheral compatibility.

title: I2C Tx DMA race condition causes no Tx-complete IRQ
body:
**Describe the set-up**
STM32H753 in custom product, compiled with arm-none-eabi-gcc 14.3 rel1

**Describe the bug**

https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx-hal-driver/blob/d649ed2c7784bfbef4be144e7bfd8dbb41dce5c3/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_i2c.c#L2055-L2076

The modification to CR1 on line 2075 races with the IRQ that is enabled on 2072.

Even though the TX DMA has not been set up, the transfer *has*. That means that the peripheral will begin the addressing phase, which may lead to a NACK interrupt.

If that NACK interrupt occurs between the read and write of the `|=` operation on 2075, then line 2075 ends up reverting the interrupt enable bits configured by the IRQ handler.

In practice, this means that the NACK and ERR interrupts are reenabled, and the STOP interrupt is cleared. This is then a critical failure because a NACK has already occurred, and the HAL needs to see a STOP in order to call the Tx complete callback.

In the end, this leads to a situation where the Tx complete callback is never called and you have to abort the HAL to get back to a working state.

**How To Reproduce**

This is heavily time dependant. This use case is with `-Og` optimisation, a 210MHz sysclk, and a 52.5MHz APB clock.

This issue can be most easily exposed by adding a delay.

Change the line:

 ```c
hi2c->Instance->CR1 |= I2C_CR1_TXDMAEN;
```

To:

```c
uint32_t const stored = hi2c->Instance->CR1;
HAL_Delay(10);
if (hi2c->Instance->CR1 != stored) {
  __BKPT();
}
hi2c->Instance->CR1 |= I2C_CR1_TXDMAEN;
```

Then perform an I2C transmit to an address that is not present on the bus, and therefore immediately generates a NACK.

If the code were race free, the transformation above would never fail. In this case it will fail reliably.

>

Hello,

I can't share much detail, but I can explain how the calls work.

We are in a FreeRTOS environment doing the following steps:

1. The thread calls `HAL_I2C_Master_Seq_Transmit_DMA`
2. The thread goes to sleep awaiting an event
3. The transmission finishes, either with `HAL_I2C_MasterTxCpltCallback` or `HAL_I2C_ErrorCallback`
4. The callback wakes up the thread
5. The thread proceeds to the next step.

In the failure case, step 3 never happens because the HAL gets stuck. The I2C peripheral is left in the following state:

- state = `HAL_I2C_STATE_BUSY_TX`
- mode = `HAL_I2C_MODE_MASTER`
- XferISR = `I2C_Master_ISR_DMA`
- Stop flag is set, all other flags are not
- NACK IE and ERR IE are enabled, all other interrupts are not
- DMA is enabled with TX complete IRQs enabled, but 16 bytes remaining in NDTR that aren't going anywhere

This is the root of why the HAL is stuck. The HAL _should_ be waiting for the STOP interrupt. But because of the race condition I described, the flags got reverted and it is waiting for the wrong IRQs.

---

I have not tried changing optimisation levels, this is being run at `-Og`.

My expectation is that the bug will exist regardless of optimisation levels (since it's a fundamental race condition), but whether you actually _see it happen_ will depend heavily on the specific timings of your project. If the clock speeds or optimisations are changed, I expect you may see the problem go away just because the timing is different. But the race condition is still there.

title: Backporting HAL FDCAN from STM32H7RS
body:
After a comparison of the FDCAN driver code between the STM32H7 and STM32H7RS, it seems to me that some functions of the STM32H7 series could be improved. Specifically:

* Initialization - `HAL_FDCAN_Init()`

`assert_param(IS_FDCAN_ALL_INSTANCE(hfdcan->Instance));` should be done before this row:
``` c
  if (hfdcan->Instance == FDCAN1)
  {
    hfdcan->ttcan = (TTCAN_TypeDef *)((uint32_t)hfdcan->Instance + 0x100U);
  }
```

* Replace raw numbers with some `#defines` (in .c and .h):
```c
#define SRAMCAN_FLS_NBR                 (128U)         /* Max. Filter List Standard Number      */
#define SRAMCAN_FLE_NBR                  (64U)         /* Max. Filter List Extended Number      */
  (etc.)

  (...)
  assert_param(IS_FDCAN_MAX_VALUE(hfdcan->Init.StdFiltersNbr, SRAMCAN_FLS_NBR));
  assert_param(IS_FDCAN_MAX_VALUE(hfdcan->Init.ExtFiltersNbr, SRAMCAN_FLE_NBR));
  (etc.)

// FDCAN_FilterTypeDef
  uint32_t FilterIndex;      /*!< Specifies the filter which will be initialized.
                                  This parameter must be a number between:
                                   - 0 and (SRAMCAN_FLS_NBR-1), if IdType is FDCAN_STANDARD_ID
                                   - 0 and (SRAMCAN_FLE_NBR-1), if IdType is FDCAN_EXTENDED_ID */

// FDCAN_RxHeaderTypeDef
  uint32_t FilterIndex;           /*!< Specifies the index of matching Rx acceptance filter element.
                                       This parameter must be a number between:
                                        - 0 and (SRAMCAN_FLS_NBR-1), if IdType is FDCAN_STANDARD_ID
                                        - 0 and (SRAMCAN_FLE_NBR-1), if IdType is FDCAN_EXTENDED_ID
                                       When the frame is a Non-Filter matching frame, this parameter
                                       is unused.                                                        */

// FDCAN_HpMsgStatusTypeDef
  uint32_t FilterIndex;    /*!< Specifies the index of matching filter element.
                                This parameter can be a number between:
                                - 0 and (SRAMCAN_FLS_NBR-1), if FilterList is 0 (Standard)
                                - 0 and (SRAMCAN_FLE_NBR-1), if FilterList is 1 (Extended) */
```

* Check `HAL_FDCAN_ConfigFilter()` when `StdFiltersNbr = 0`:

```c
STM32H7
  assert_param(IS_FDCAN_MAX_VALUE(sFilterConfig->FilterIndex, (hfdcan->Init.StdFiltersNbr - 1U)));

STM32H7RS
  assert_param(IS_FDCAN_MAX_VALUE((sFilterConfig->FilterIndex + 1U), hfdcan->Init.StdFiltersNbr));
```
 
* Some timeout functions for STM32H7 use the `FDCAN_TIMEOUT_COUNT  (50U)` value but in STM32H7RS still use `FDCAN_TIMEOUT_VALUE  (10U)`

* Fix typo `FDCAN_CalcultateRamBlockAddresses()` -> `FDCAN_CalculateRamBlockAddresses()`

title: AES GCM Invalid Tag Generation after Decryption
body:
**Describe the bug**
An invalid tag is generated for payloads that are not a multiple of 4, as described in [Re: STM32U545 AES GCM Tag mismatch - STMicroelectronics Community](https://community.st.com/t5/stm32-mcus-security/stm32h730-aes-gcm-tag-issue/m-p/806718/highlight/true#M8519).

ST Internal ticket number: **210917**.

**How To Reproduce**
An example STM32Cube-IDE project is generated with STM32CubeMX and attached in the mentioned [community thread](https://community.st.com/t5/stm32-mcus-security/stm32h730-aes-gcm-tag-issue/m-p/807226/highlight/true#M8522).

**Describe the set-up**
Custom board with STM32H730XX.

AES GCM encryption and decryption are performed with settings:
```
DataType = CRYP_DATATYPE_8B
DataWidthUnit  = CRYP_DATAWIDTHUNIT_BYTE
KeySize = CRYP_KEYSIZE_128B
HeaderWidthUnit = CRYP_HEADERWIDTHUNIT_BYTE
```

**Additional context**

Tag is generated correctly when:
* When the input array is 16 bytes, but we decode 15 bytes (_as there is only 15 bytes of data_).
* When we dynamically allocate an aligned input array of size that is a multiple of _4_,
   but decode with real size (_i.e, 15_).
* When the input array is in the global scope (_regardless of its size_).

The tag is generated incorrectly:
* When the input array is 15 bytes on the stack.

Tried to flush and invalidate the input memory area, as well as to flush ECC (_as buffers are located within SRAM with enabled ECC)_, no difference.

After further investigation, the culprit seems to be the padding bytes.

During the encryption, the `CRYP_CR_NPBLB` is used to let HW know which bytes to discard;
However, during the decryption process, it is not used/or available.

Here is the debug info, which shows that the input with 16 bytes has explicit `00` padding in the last word (`0x00a989d1`); whereas when the input buffer is 15 bytes, we get `8a` instead of `00` in the last word (`0x8aa989d1`).

Working with 16 length:

```gdb
x/15xb hcryp->pCrypInBuffPtr
0x2402a5d8: 0x13    0xb4    0xc7    0x2b    0x38    0x9d    0xc5    0x01
0x2402a5e0: 0x8e    0x72    0xa1    0x71    0xd1    0x89    0xa9

x/4xw hcryp->pCrypInBuffPtr
0x2402a5d8: 0x2bc7b413  0x01c59d38  0x71a1728e  0x00a989d1

When CrypInCount == 3
p/x *(uint32_t *)(hcryp->pCrypInBuffPtr + hcryp->CrypInCount)
$2 = 0xa989d1
```

Not working with 15 length:

```gdb
x/15xb hcryp->pCrypInBuffPtr
0x24021c54: 0x13    0xb4    0xc7    0x2b    0x38    0x9d    0xc5    0x01
0x24021c5c: 0x8e    0x72    0xa1    0x71    0xd1    0x89    0xa9

x/4xw hcryp->pCrypInBuffPtr
0x24021c54: 0x2bc7b413  0x01c59d38  0x71a1728e  0x8aa989d1
```

After correction of the padding in the last block (_16 bytes_) of the last writable word (_4 bytes_) the tag generation works fine after decryption, required changes are applied to `CRYP_AESGCM_Process` in `stm32h7xx_hal_cryp.c`:

```diff
--- a/stm32cube/stm32h7xx/drivers/src/stm32h7xx_hal_cryp.c
+++ b/stm32cube/stm32h7xx/drivers/src/stm32h7xx_hal_cryp.c
@@ -3085,10 +3085,17 @@ static HAL_StatusTypeDef CRYP_AESGCM_Process(CRYP_HandleTypeDef *hcryp, uint32_t
       }
 
       /* Write the last input block in the IN FIFO */
+      unsigned pad_bytes = ((((uint32_t)(hcryp->Size) / 4U) + 1U) * 4U) - (uint32_t)(hcryp->Size);
       for (index = 0U; index < lastwordsize; index ++)
       {
-        hcryp->Instance->DIN  = *(uint32_t *)(hcryp->pCrypInBuffPtr + hcryp->CrypInCount);
-        hcryp->CrypInCount++;
+          if (((hcryp->Instance->CR & CRYP_CR_ALGODIR) == CRYP_OPERATINGMODE_DECRYPT) &&
+              (((pad_bytes != 0)) && (index + 1 == lastwordsize))) {
+            // set pad bytes to 0
+            hcryp->Instance->DIN = (*(uint32_t *)(hcryp->pCrypInBuffPtr + hcryp->CrypInCount) << (pad_bytes * 8)) >> (pad_bytes * 8);
+          } else {
+            hcryp->Instance->DIN  = *(uint32_t *)(hcryp->pCrypInBuffPtr + hcryp->CrypInCount);
+          }
+          hcryp->CrypInCount++;
       }
``` 

PS: Although the fix appears to work (_tested with input data of 15 and 42 bytes, with and without AD of size 13 and 20 bytes_), I'm uncertain if it's entirely correct; therefore, I'm opening this as an issue. I can also submit a PR if needed.

title: HAL_I2C_Mem_Read_DMA should call I2C_Enable_IRQ with flag I2C_XFER_RX_IT instead of I2C_XFER_TX_IT
body:
**Describe the set-up**
 * Board: F7 nucleo board

**Describe the bug**
Bug comes when there is a `HAL_I2C_Mem_Read_DMA` followed by `HAL_I2C_Mem_Write`. 

1. When `I2C_Enable_IRQ` is called with flag `I2C_XFER_TX_IT`, after DMA read is done, TXIS is still enabled.
2. Later call of blocking write function `HAL_I2C_Mem_Write` will trigger the `I2Cx_EV_IRQHandler`, while XferISR will be NULL, so again TXIS will not get cleared, and the  `I2Cx_EV_IRQHandler` will be entered/exit infinitely. This makes other lower priority interrupts and application codes will not get executed.

**How To Reproduce**
1. Call `HAL_I2C_Mem_Read_DMA`
2. call `HAL_I2C_Mem_Write`
3. check if `I2Cx_EV_IRQHandler` is executed infinitely.

title: HAL_ETH_ReleaseTxPacket() can present the PTP TX timestamp of a different packet to the application code if preempted
body:
I described several locking and concurrency problems of HAL_ETH in issue #72 #71 #70 and #69. This is another one related to the improper or missing locking via `gState `and `HAL_ETH_STATE_BUSY`.

If `HAL_ETH_ReleaseTxPacket()` gets preempted and another call to itself in another threads get scheduled (the functions is racing with itself), then the PTP timestamps stored in `heth->TxTimestamp` may be overwritten with those of another packet before the application callback `HAL_ETH_TxPtpCallback()` or `heth->txPtpCallback()` in the original call to `HAL_ETH_ReleaseTxPacket()` gets executed.

https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx_hal_driver/blob/ceda3ceeca2ee77a76d2de2ee6b560ad87c90a48/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_eth.c#L1437-L1467

This would cause the application code to read the overwritten PTP timestamp and not the timestamp of the packet it actually sent.

This problem could be solved by either locking properly and atomically via gState or by not storing the timestamp in `heth->TxTimestamp` but in a stack variable in `HAL_ETH_ReleaseTxPacket()` and handing that stack pointer to the application which would be unique per thread.

comments.author: ASEHSTM
comments.body:
Hello @KarstenHohmeier,

Thank you for your report. The HAL library is often used in contexts where the end user manages the synchronization of calls to HAL functions. If your application operates in a multi-threaded environment, we recommend using external synchronization mechanisms, such as mutexes or semaphores, to protect calls to `HAL_ETH_ReleaseTxPacket()`.

With Regards,

title: HAL_ETH_ReleaseTxPacket() does not test gState and races with itself and TX functions when accessing TX descriptors and counters
body:
HAL_ETH_ReleaseTxPacket() does **NOT** check gState before execution **AT ALL**.

https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx_hal_driver/blob/ceda3ceeca2ee77a76d2de2ee6b560ad87c90a48/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_eth.c#L1400-L1413

It just runs and modifies TX descriptors, decrements buffer counters and reads state from &heth into local variables.
This buffered state can become stale/outdated if HAL_ETH_ReleaseTxPacket() gets preempted and other threads issuing calls to HAL_ETH_Transmit_IT() or HAL_ETH_Transmit() get scheduled instead.

Among other things HAL_ETH_ReleaseTxPacket() contains the decrement of `dmatxdesclist->BuffersInUse`.

https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx_hal_driver/blob/ceda3ceeca2ee77a76d2de2ee6b560ad87c90a48/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_eth.c#L1477

for which the increment has been guarded by a critical section

https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx_hal_driver/blob/ceda3ceeca2ee77a76d2de2ee6b560ad87c90a48/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_eth.c#L3333-L3340

So somebody suspected there might be race conditions there but failed to follow through ;)

You really, really, really need to lock this properly with atomic Test-and-Set of gState, because even the read-modify-write of TX descriptor OWN bits is potentially racy (see #71 #70 and #69)

This is not a theoretical bug! Under high incoming packet load (~8000 packets per second RX) there are frequent preemptions by the input thread which runs with realtime priority (code generated by CubeIDE).

![grafik](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f3a52b25-3eaf-4ad7-90fe-6b3d20e4e569)

This causes the TX calls and TX packet releases in other threads to be preempted and scheduled randomly and thrashes the data in &heth to a point where the system would not send TX packets any more. Under low packet load this can still occur and leads to unstable TX operation where systems will stop transmitting data after multiple days when these race conditions randomly occur but with much lower probability.

title: HAL_ETH does non-atomic Test-and-Set operations on gState which is not thread-safe
body:
HAL_ETH uses gState as a "poor man's mutex" to guard it's internal state and associated hardware registers against concurrent access and enforce a specific order of initialization.

When gState gets tested and set to BUSY for example, HAL_ETH does critical things to its own state or the hardware:

https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx_hal_driver/blob/ceda3ceeca2ee77a76d2de2ee6b560ad87c90a48/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_eth.c#L863-L866

Yet these test and set operations are not done atomically (e.g. inside a critical section) so the HAL_ETH locking via gState is vulnerable to race conditions in situations with preemption (e.g. with lwIP + FreeRTOS)

comments.author: ASEHSTM
comments.body:
Hello @KarstenHohmeier,

Thank you for your contribution. This function has been reliably used in previous projects without any race condition issues, and tests show that the code functions correctly. 
Interrupts are disabled to prevent any interference during critical operations via the `__HAL_ETH_DMA_DISABLE_IT` function at line 873, which includes transmission, reception, and fatal bus interrupts. 

If this point has caused you any issues, please inform us about your specific use case. We remain open to further discussion.

Thank you for your understanding and cooperation.
With Regards

comments.author: KarstenHohmeier
comments.body:
The code referenced is a general example of the code-pattern ST Micro uses to deal with concurrency and locking inside HAL_ETH. 

The real issues arise in the TX and RX functions in HAL_ETH where you omit this locking pattern entirely or execute this Test-and-Set pattern only half-way (test for STARTED but no set to BUSY) see #71 and #72.

If you would try and fix #71 and #72 by using the gState locking pattern - as you do throughout HAL_ETH - it would still not be entirely thread-safe because you don't do it atomically. This is what this issue is about. To remind you of the locking pattern you seem to use and make the case that it is conceptually broken by being non-atomic and would thus not be suitable (without being fixed itself) for fixing the real concurrency issues related to the TX and RX function (#71, #72).

This is also not something your tests would show. The realization as a developer that non-atomic test-and-set of a locking variable is flawed and should be fixed regardless of prior track record or existing tests.

comments.author: ASEHSTM
comments.body:
Hello @KarstenHohmeier,

The HAL driver is designed to be a generic library, usable in a variety of projects, whether they use an RTOS or not. This flexibility means that certain responsibilities, such as managing race conditions, are delegated to the end user. 
This approach helps maintain the lightness and simplicity of the HAL code. Systematically adding critical sections or synchronization primitives to the HAL code could introduce performance overhead and additional complexity. 

In many cases, users do not need these mechanisms, especially in non-preemptive environments or simple applications.

With Regards,

comments.author: KarstenHohmeier
comments.body:
If you do not guarantee thread-safety for HAL_ETH - which is a valid design decision - then you should add this as a giant warning to the API / function descriptions.

Also you should probably talk to your colleagues that are responsible for generating `ethernetif.c` when setting up a H7-project from CubeIDE with LWIP and FreeRTOS. 

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5fe3b41a-2407-4523-aef6-ecf5a35f07fc)

If you are right, then the code they generate for `low_level_input()` and `low_level_output()` does not use HAL_ETH in a thread-safe manner for H7 projects which results in a "sub-optimal user experience" ;)

`ethernetif.c` is where I fixed the issue for our project - by scrapping the generated ST code and wrapping the HAL_ETH calls and associated critical operations into a mutex.

To think a little more about "non-preemptive environments": Imagine a scenario without preemption (no RTOS) where the user code runs in a main-loop and sends one TX packet every second. Then you connect a button to the system that triggers an interrupt and sends a time-critical notification packet directly from the IRQ handler. You would expect this to be ok, since the packets are handed to the DMA via descriptor lists. But effectively your IRQ code is preempting the main-loop and might cause the same concurrency issues that RTOS preemption would if the calls to HAL_ETH are not thread-safe. This gets even worse with nested IRQs where even interrupts can be interrupted. So even in a bare-metal scenario with only IRQs the user would have to guard the HAL_ETH usage themselves to make it function correctly under all circumstances. So whatever performance you think you gain by omitting thread-safety cannot be gained "legitimately" because the user has to add back thread-safety in the user code.

But this is more thought experiment and colored by my opinion. I am sure you will do the right thing and sort this out in a sensible fashion and thank you for taking these bug reports seriously.

body:
Looking at HAL_ETH I noticed that these defines for the HAL_ETH global state (gState) have the same value (0x23):

https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx_hal_driver/blob/ceda3ceeca2ee77a76d2de2ee6b560ad87c90a48/Inc/stm32h7xx_hal_eth.h#L1474-L1478

Also the comments associated with these values are wrong/misleading. Maybe you can improve on these a little.
Here is how I understand the values after looking at how they are used in the code:

- HAL_ETH_STATE_RESET means: heth private data is not initialized at all, please call HAL_ETH_Init()
- HAL_ETH_STATE_READY means: you can register callbacks now, but to start the actual hardware and the interrupts please call HAL_ETH_Start() or HAL_ETH_Start_IT()
- HAL_ETH_STATE_STARTED means: heth is running and ready for RX and TX operations
- HAL_ETH_STATE_BUSY means: heth is currently doing something 'critical' that should not be done concurrently, because it would mess up the internal state of heth or the hardware
- HAL_ETH_STATE_ERROR means: heth encountered an error that needs external handling; see HAL_ETH_ErrorCallback() and HAL_ETH_DeInit()

title: Ethernet tail pointer setup is incorrect, and tail pointer management does not work with timestamping enabled
body:
**Describe the set-up**
Any Stm32H7

**Describe the bug**
The RX tail pointer is set in both ETH_UpdateDescriptor() (called on init by HAL_ETH_Start_IT()) and ETH_DMARxDescListInit() (called by HAL_ETH_Init()). 

The updating of the tail pointer in  ETH_UpdateDescriptor() is a runtime update, and the tail pointer will be set to the last descriptor processed by the app. When the descriptors are initially built (from the call in HAL_ETH_Start_IT()), the tail pointer will be set to 1. This is not the correct value for it to be set to on init, and this would mean that only 1 descriptor would be available. ST was clearly trying to init this tail pointer to the correct value in ETH_DMARxDescListInit(), but this function call happens **before* the call to build the descriptors via ETH_UpdateDescriptor() from the call to HAL_ETH_Start_IT() so the tail pointer is effectively initialized incorrectly. 

IF timestamping is enabled, at least 2 descriptors will be needed by the very first packet which arrives. This will cause an RBU.

**How To Reproduce**
1. Indicate the global behavior of your application project
RBU because only one descriptor is available. 

3. The modules that you suspect to be the cause of the problem (Driver, BSP, MW ...)
Eth

4. The use case that generates the problem
Any use where more than one single descriptor is needed in the first packet

6. How we can reproduce the problem
Look at the code, confirm that the tail pointer is being initialized to the incorrect value during init building after it was supposed to have been set to the right value.

**Describe the set-up**
Custom board or nucleo, 

**Describe the bug**
In HAL_ETH_ReadData(), the ptp timestamp retrieval is completely incorrect. If timestamping is enabled, is at least one descriptor is given by DMA which is the normal descriptor. Then, the next descriptor following it will be the context descriptor. The way the HAL_ETH_ReadData() function is written, it will exit as soon as it sees a normal descriptor (rxdataready will be set to 1). The next call of the function would then read the context, but one single call to this function should read both the normal packet information AND the timestamp data for that packet.

NA

4. How we can reproduce the problem
Enable timestamping, notice you need two calls to HAL_ETH_ReadData() to get the packet first, then the timestamp second

**Additional context**
ST needs to pay attention when writing peripheral drivers. The reason for this issue is that the MAC IP block for the Stm32F7 (and similar parts) works differently. The timestamp comes in as an extension to a normal descriptor (An "enhanced" descriptor"). This means that it's not an extra descriptor which is generated, which is *unlike* the Stm32H7's MAC IP block (which makes an additional "context" descriptor"). This is clearly a copy and paste error.  Additionally, this is evidence that ST didn't test the PTP functionality, because they would have immediately noticed this issue.

title: HAL_DMA_Abort_IT leaves handle in aborted state
body:
There seems to be an inconsistency in the HAL_DMA_Abort_IT() function:

- if you abort a DMA1 or DMA2 transfer then the handle gets left in the HAL_DMA_STATE_ABORT state and the abort callback is not called. The handle is not usable without reinitialising.
- if you are using a BDMA instance then the handle state gets left in HAL_DMA_STATE_READY, the abort callback is called. The handle is immediately reusable.

title: Need for HAL_SPI_TransmitFollowedByReceive function
body:
When working with SPI slave devices, a quite common scenario is reading some data from the slave.
This iks usually done by a single SPI transaction made by:
- sending data to the slave (i.e., specifying which data master wants to read)
- reading data from the slave
while the NSS pin stays asserted.
As an example  see the following screenshot:
![immagine](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx_hal_driver/assets/22594460/42fbd903-954d-42ea-8ed6-e577a3299d2f)

From the programmer side, I usually have:
- data to be written already filled in a buffer `tx_buf` of size `tx_size`
- a buffer `rx_buf` of size `rx_size` to be filled with the data read from the slave

With HAL SPI, if I want to use a `HAL_SPI_Transmit()` followed by a `HAL_SPI_Receive()` I must use NSS pin driven by software, otherwise it's deasserted at the end of `HAL_SPI_Transmit()` and re-asserted before `HAL_SPI_Receive()`.
But this is not what the slave needs (NSS must stay asserted).
Handling it by software (driving the GPIO pin high or low) works, but it requires time between tx and rx, and this decreases the "real" baud rate.

If I want to use `HAL_SPI_TransmitReceive()`, it requires two buffers (`pTxData` and `pRxData`) and both of them must have size `tx_size + rx_size`.
Probably I can use a single buffer passing it to `pTxData` and `pRxData` input parameters, but it must have a size of `tx_size + rx_size`, and from the application side it's not so common.
As I wrote above, there is one `tx_buf` of size `tx_size` and onther `rx_buf` of size `rx_size`.

I don't know if this is a good idea, but I think that a new function with the following prototype
```
HAL_StatusTypeDef HAL_SPI_TransmitFollowedByReceive(SPI_HandleTypeDef *hspi, const uint8_t *pTxData, uint16_t txSize,
                                          uint8_t *pRxData, uint16_t rxSize, uint32_t Timeout);
```
would be ok.
And it would be responsible to assert NSS before starting tx and deasserting it after the end of rx, if NSS is driven by hardware.

Does this suggestion sound good?
Or is there a simpler way to do this?

title: Incorrect assertion in HAL_ADC_ConfigChannel() for STM32H7
body:
**Description of the set-up**
* STM32H753
* CubeMX 6.6.1
* STM32H7 HAL v1.11.0

**Description of the bug**

The function `HAL_ADC_ConfigChannel()` contains the following check:
```c
  /* if ROVSE is set, the value of the OFFSETy_EN bit in ADCx_OFRy register is
     ignored (considered as reset) */
  assert_param(!((sConfig->OffsetNumber != ADC_OFFSET_NONE) && (hadc->Init.OversamplingMode == ENABLE)));
```

I guess the assertion is (incorrectly) copied from the STM32L4 (or other device) HAL code, for which this check is correct. The STM32L4+ reference manual (RM0432 Rev 9) states the following, which matches the description in the code comment:
> Offset correction is not supported in oversampling mode. When ROVSE and/or JOVSE bit isset, the value of the OFFSETy_EN bit in ADC_OFRy register is ignored (considered as reset).

However, according to the reference manual (RM0433 Rev 7):
> The offset correction is also supported in oversampling mode.

Since the offset correction is also supported in oversampling mode on the STM32H753, this assertion is incorrect and should be removed or modified (`OffsetRightShift` and `OffsetSignedSaturation` are not supported in oversampling mode, so probably those should be checked instead).

**How To Reproduce**

Call `HAL_ADC_ConfigChannel()` with `sConfig->OffsetNumber` defined to another value then `ADC_OFFSET_NONE` (e.g. `ADC_OFFSET_1`) and `hadc->Init.OversamplingMode` set to `ENABLE` and `USE_FULL_ASSERT` defined.

title: Incorrect ADC calibration factor size
body:
The macro `IS_ADC_CALFACT` is currently defined (see [here](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx_hal_driver/blob/12ae8efadd6d8904476b5fbd319e1c266afce734/Inc/stm32h7xx_hal_adc_ex.h#L925)) as:
```c
#define IS_ADC_CALFACT(__CALIBRATION_FACTOR__) ((__CALIBRATION_FACTOR__) <= (0x7FU))
```

This macro is used to check the parameters of `HAL_ADCEx_Calibration_SetValue` (see [here](https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx_hal_driver/blob/12ae8efadd6d8904476b5fbd319e1c266afce734/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_adc_ex.c#L270)):

```c
  assert_param(IS_ADC_CALFACT(CalibrationFactor));
```

Consequently, when `USE_FULL_ASSERT` is enabled in the HAL, the assertion is violated when using a calibration factor with a value larger than 127.

However, the calibration factor is 11 bits, so I think the check should be `<= 0x7FFU`.

**Patch**

The corrected code should be:
```c
/**
  * @brief Calibration factor size verification (11 bits maximum).
  * @param __CALIBRATION_FACTOR__ Calibration factor value.
  * @retval SET (__CALIBRATION_FACTOR__ is within the authorized size) or RESET (__CALIBRATION_FACTOR__ is too large)
  */
#define IS_ADC_CALFACT(__CALIBRATION_FACTOR__) ((__CALIBRATION_FACTOR__) <= 0x7FFU)
```

Note that the documentation of `HAL_ADCEx_Calibration_SetValue` also mentions the 7 bits maximum instead of 11 bits maximum:
```none
  * @param CalibrationFactor Calibration factor (coded on 7 bits maximum)
```
should be:

```none
  * @param CalibrationFactor Calibration factor (coded on 11 bits maximum)
```

title: DMA2D_IRQHandler called with empty ISR register
body:
I'm using a custom board with STM32H723 (144pin), 5inch display (LTDC), external SRAM (FMC), external NOR flash (OSPI) with Touchgfx and DMA2D (double buffer strategy). No OS.

I experimented **random stucks of the touchgfx** like described in [this](https://community.st.com/s/question/0D53W00000e067WSAQ/ui-stuck-in-takeframebuffersemaphore) thread. After struggling I found out that the problem was caused by **DMA2D_IRQHandler called with empty ISR register**. In fact, the touchgfx was expecting a call to _XferErrorCallback(hdma2d)_ that never happened and so hanged on.

For what I've seen when this _empty call_ is triggered the _DMA2D_FLAG_TC_ should be HIGH, but actually this sometimes doesn't happens.

I do not know why this happens (silicon bug? touchgfx clean the flag in particular moment?), but for sure the HAL library doesn't manage this case.

So to solve my issue I changed in `void HAL_DMA2D_IRQHandler(DMA2D_HandleTypeDef *hdma2d){...}` of _stm32h7xx_hal_dma2d.c_ the following line:
`if ((isrflags & DMA2D_FLAG_TC) != 0U)`
in
`if ((isrflags & DMA2D_FLAG_TC) != 0U || isrflags == 0U)`

**Additional context**

title: HAL_UART_RegisterRxEventCallback fails if there is a transmit ongoing
body:
**Description**
It is impossible to set an RxEventCallback (with `HAL_UART_RegisterRxEventCallback`) if a transmit is active on the port.

**How To Reproduce**
start a UART transmit with `HAL_UART_Transmit_IT`. 
then immediately thereafter call `HAL_UART_RegisterRxEventCallback`. That call _will_ fail.

**Analysis**
This is caused by the fact that `HAL_UART_RegisterRxEventCallback` checks the value of the `gState` field instead of the `RxState` like all other receive releated functions do. I don't see a reason for this difference. As far is I can tell the RxEventCallback is unrelated to transmit so checking `gState` appears to be a mistake.

**My Solution**
Changing `gState` in `HAL_UART_RegisterRxEventCallback` and `HAL_UART_UnregisterRxEventCallback` to `RxState` makes the problem go away, as expected. And it did not cause unwanted side effects in my testing.

title: Padding warnings that need fix
body:
When the source code is comèpiled with armclang with all the warnbings enabled, some padding warnings are shown.
I think that "zero compiler warnings" with very strict compilation flags is an ambitious, but really appreciated target from the user point of view.

Here are some of these needed paddings:
`.../STM32H7xx_HAL_Driver/Inc\stm32h7xx_hal_uart.h(234): warning: padding struct 'struct __UART_HandleTypeDef' with 2 bytes to align 'FifoMode' [-Wpadded]`
So
`uint16_t                 padding;`
is needed just before
https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx_hal_driver/blob/8e7eb8dba8bee5e4c260c6fc724437502e98fc76/Inc/stm32h7xx_hal_uart.h#L233-L234

`.../STM32H7xx_HAL_Driver/Inc\stm32h7xx_hal_uart.h(253): warning: padding struct 'struct __UART_HandleTypeDef' with 3 bytes to align 'gState' [-Wpadded]`
So
`uint8_t                 padding_bytes[3];`
should be needed just before
https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx_hal_driver/blob/8e7eb8dba8bee5e4c260c6fc724437502e98fc76/Inc/stm32h7xx_hal_uart.h#L252-L254
But I think that this depends on the behavior of the compiler, because `HAL_LockTypeDef` is an `enum` and so every compiler can set its size to different values.
Maybe an union to a fixed size value is the best option?

comments.author: wovano
comments.body:
I generally agree with the wish to support warning-free compilation, but in this case it simply means that [you've turned on too many warnings](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/20184259/what-does-the-padding-class-tester-with-4-bytes-warning-mean#comment30091914_20184259) (see also [here](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/40662265/warning-for-struct-padding-in-clang)). This is not a compiler warning that indicates a (possible) problem with the code, but simply an extra diagnostic that is disabled by default (and even when using `-Wall`).

Manually adding padding bytes will only obfuscate the code and does not solve any problem (other than suppressing this warning that you specifically enabled).

The point of this compiler warning is to be aware of memory wasted due to struct padding. Manually added dummy variables will waste the same amount of memory but hide it from the compiler. The real solution would be to reorder the struct members from large to small so the amount of padding bytes is actually minimized. This would reduce the struct size from 144 to 140 bytes (or from 200 to 196 bytes if callbacks are enabled), which is quite insignificant. If memory constraints are that important, the low-level HAL would probably be a better match. For the HAL, readability/understandability and maintainability are more important and I doubt this proposal would really benefit anyone.

My 2 cents.

title: Missing ReceiveToIdle API in HAL USART
body: There doesn't seem to be a ReceiveToIdle API for the USART devices while there is one for UART devices. This is an issue when, in my case for board layout reasons, switching from UART to USART. The peripheral does support it, it's just missing in HAL.

comments.author: ASELSTM
comments.body:
Hi @sdekrijger,

First, thank you for your contribution. The objective of the ReceiveToIdle APIs is to allow application to handle use cases where number of data to be received is unknown. It is useful for the UART case as communication is asynchronous, the Transmitter and Receiver don't share a clock reference. Therefore, unless a start bit detected, the receiver does not know exactly when it will receive a data.

For USART case this can be driven by the CLK synchronization signal. As long as there is data to be received as long as there is signal on the CLK pin. Once no more activity is detected on the clock line, thus reception is over. As per referenced in the reference manual :

> In master mode, the SCLK pin operates in conjunction with the TX pin. Thus, the clock is provided only if the transmitter is enabled (TE=1) and data are being transmitted (USART_TDR data register written). 

The clock signal can then provide an overview of the data transfer status, even if the amount of data to be received is unknown.

Hence, we do not have plans to add ReceiveToIdle APIs for the USART driver.  Please allow me then to close this issue. Thank you for your comprehension and thank you once again for your contribution.

With regards,

title: Ethernet: Add ability to explicitly free specific descriptors or release descriptor with new address
body:
In embedded IP stack usage (e.g. lwip), which is typically implemented as zero-copy, the presently available interfaces for recycling RxDescriptors is problematic. Ideally, when a packet is received and read out of the HAL, the driver code would pass this buffer to the stack, and would only release the descriptor back to the HAL driver when the stack releases this buffer (e.g. through a `pbuf_free()` call).  Between pushing this message into the stack, and the stack _freeing_ this buffer back to the driver (and thus the descriptor to the HAL), it's possible that additional packets are received that go through this same process.

Given the scenario above, in a multi-threaded environment, there is no way to guarantee the order the packets are _freed_ is the same order in which they are _received_. The only support approach in the HAL driver is to free all consumed RX descriptors through the `HAL_ETH_BuildRxDescriptors()` call, but as the freeing may happen in a different order, this approach may cause descriptors to get re-used before the data has been consumed.

Ideally, the user would be able to release RX descriptors in any order and as singalled by the stack through `pbuf_free()` like calls.  A few possible ideas for this would be...


1. Simplest API would be to release the last descriptor (single), but with a new buffer address, for example `HAL_ETH_ReleaseOneRxDescriptor(ETH_HandleTypeDef *heth, void *new_buffer_address)`. This could optionally be extended to take an array or even something like an `ETH_BufferTypeDef` linked list, `HAL_ETH_ReleaseRxDescriptors(ETH_HandleTypeDef *heth, ETH_BufferTypeDef *buffers)` although implementing this from the user code with multiple calls to `ReleaseOne` might actually be a little more straightforward than creating the linked list.

1. API such as `HAL_ETH_ReleaseRxDescriptor(ETH_HandleTypeDef *heth, uint32_t index)`.  For this API to work, the user would need to be able to also get the descriptor indices associated with the  for `HAL_ETH_GetRxDataBuffer()` possibly it could be embedded in the `ETH_BufferTypeDef` or through a separate `HAL_ETH_GetRxDescriptorInfo()` such that it could then be tracked and freed when available.

I have following additional information to share:

After reviewing the inputs that I've received, I had a quick glance at the STM32G4 Series Reference manual, April 2020, RM0440, Rev 3. I tried searching for FDCAN_CCU_IR or its alias CCU_IR, but I was unable to find it. Hence, my conclusion is that ONLY STM32G4XX code does not have to use the FDCAN_IR_MASK (as it helps break down value parts that is to be written to FDCAN_IR and FDCAN_CCU_IR).

I understand writing 1 to a bit of FDCAN_CCU_IR and FDCAN_IR will only clear them. Writing 0 to any bit does not have any impact. However, this is not the case with FDCAN_CCU_IE and FDCAN_IE

Hence, I request that all four macros namely __HAL_FDCAN_ENABLE_IT(),  __HAL_FDCAN_DISABLE_IT(), __HAL_FDCAN_CLEAR_IT() and __HAL_FDCAN_CLEAR_FLAG() be modified, so as to have different macros which independently take care of FDCAN_CCU_IX (where X = E or R) and FDCAN_IX (where X = E or R).

As on day the bits [31:30] of FDCAN_IX are unused, hence the coder is left shifting the FDCAN_CCU_IX bits (where X = E or R) by 30 before passing as a value to the existing macros.

What if these reserved bits [31:30] of FDCAN_IX are used for some interrupt in future, then the current implementation will become a BAD Implementation. Hence it will be good if either 8 bytes (i.e. 4 for FDCAN_IX and 4 for FDCAN_CCU_IX) or structure variable is passed to the macros so that there is not any adverse impact while making changes to the register values.

comments.author: rxa1031
comments.body: Basically one should be able to update FDCAN_CCU_IE and FDCAN_IE mutually exclusively.

comments.author: ALABSTM
comments.body:
Hi @rxa1031,

I hope you are doing well. As for your concerns:
* As for the macro `__HAL_FDCAN_CLEAR_FLAG()` (the same applies to the macro `__HAL_FDCAN_ENABLE_IT`), it has been defined to handle **both** registers `FDCAN_IR` and `FDCANCCU_IR` using **one signle** parameter `__FLAG__`:
  * As you pointed out, register `FDCAN_IR` has **2** reserved bits (30 and 31), while register `FDCANCCU_IR` has only **2** used bits (0 and 1).
  * The idea is that parameter `__FLAG__` is made up of two parts:
    * bits 0 to 29 holding data to be written in register `FDCAN_IR`.
    * bits 30 and 31 holding data to be written in register `FDCANCCU_IR`.
  * The two parts of the `__FLAG__` parameters are extracted thanks to the masks  `FDCAN_IR_MASK` and `CCU_IR_MASK` as shown in the code snippets below. Notice also the **shift** to the right before the storage in the `FDCANCCU_IR` register.
  * I agree with you that if one day bits 30 and 31 of register are to be used, the code implementation has to be changed. However, this can be made in a way **totally transparent** to the user and with **preserving** backward compatibility.

https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx_hal_driver/blob/d8461b980b59b1625207d8c4f2ce0a9c2a7a3b04/Inc/stm32h7xx_hal_fdcan.h#L1528-L1529
https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx_hal_driver/blob/d8461b980b59b1625207d8c4f2ce0a9c2a7a3b04/Inc/stm32h7xx_hal_fdcan.h#L1855-L1859

* As for the variables `TxEventFifoITs`, `RxFifo0Its`, and `RxFifo1Its`, and their use within the callbacks, this is up to the user to decide of the way they see it best appropriate to use them. This includes shifting their content by 4 or by 8.
Regarding the shifting itself, I am tempted to think it can be avoided:
  * Indeed, within each one of the above mentioned variables, bit positions are preserved thanks to the masks used, as shown in the code snippets below.
  * These masks being defined using the **CMSIS bits** definitions, we could think about using them directly as suggested at the end of this comment.

https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx_hal_driver/blob/d8461b980b59b1625207d8c4f2ce0a9c2a7a3b04/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_fdcan.c#L210
https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32h7xx_hal_driver/blob/d8461b980b59b1625207d8c4f2ce0a9c2a7a3b04/Src/stm32h7xx_hal_fdcan.c#L5273-L5274

```c
void HAL_FDCAN_RxFifo1Callback(FDCAN_HandleTypeDef *hfdcan, uint32_t RxFifo1ITs)
{

  ...

  if ((RxFifo1ITs & FDCAN_IR_RF0L) != 0U)
  {
    /* Treatment in case of FDCAN_IR_RF0L interrupt */
  }

  ...
}
```

I hope this answers your questions. Thank you again for having shared your concerns. Please allow me to close this issue now.

With regards,
